abstract: Dr. Hildebrand presents a systematic approach to diagnosing and managing rheumatoid arthritis (RA) in a family medicine setting, emphasizing the use of ACR criteria rather than memorization. She reviews key history features (morning stiffness >6 weeks, small joint involvement), physical exam findings (synovitis, boggy joints), and appropriate lab testing (RF, anti-CCP, ESR, CRP) while cautioning against indiscriminate ANA ordering. Treatment initiation with methotrexate, including baseline screening and dose titration based on ESR, is discussed, along with the importance of referral to rheumatology. The lecture also briefly touches on lupus and the value of clinical reasoning over exhaustive testing.
key_points: RA diagnosis requires symptoms lasting at least six weeks, with morning stiffness and small joint involvement as key triggers.
Use the ACR 2010 criteria (joint involvement, serology, acute phase reactants, duration) to systematically classify RA; a score ≥6 indicates definite RA.
Physical exam should assess for synovitis (warm, boggy, tender joints) and compare to unaffected joints; absence of synovitis makes RA less likely.
Order RF, anti-CCP, ESR, and CRP; avoid ordering ANA unless lupus is specifically suspected due to high false-positive rates.
High-positive RF and anti-CCP (e.g., >3x upper limit) are strongly supportive of RA.
Before starting methotrexate, screen for TB, HIV, hepatitis B/C, and check baseline liver and renal function.
Start methotrexate at a low dose and titrate every 2-4 weeks based on ESR response; disease activity is reassessed at 3 months.
If rheumatology access is delayed, initiate methotrexate and refer concurrently; steroids can be used for symptom relief while waiting.
Psoriatic arthritis should be considered if nail pitting or distal joint involvement is present; fibromyalgia is a diagnosis of exclusion.
Lupus can present with pleuritic chest pain, rash, photosensitivity, and low complement; use SLICC criteria if suspected.
Fatigue workup should include CBC, TSH, and a comprehensive metabolic panel (chem 14).
Small joint pain (DIP, PIP, MCP) with fatigue can be a presenting symptom of autoimmune disease.
